final_proof:
Let \(R=\mathbb Z_p=\{x\in\mathbb Q_p:|x|_p\le 1\}\). We use the standard normalization \(|p|_p=p^{-1}\). Recall that for every nonzero \(x\in\mathbb Q_p\), its valuation \(v_p(x)\) is an integer and \(|x|_p=p^{-v_p(x)}\).

First, \(R\) is a commutative ring with identity. Certainly \(0,1\in R\). If \(x,y\in R\), then the ultrametric inequality and multiplicativity of the norm give
\[
|x-y|_p\le\max\{|x|_p,|y|_p\}\le1,\qquad |xy|_p=|x|_p|y|_p\le1.
\]
Thus \(x-y,xy\in R\), proving the assertion.

Define
\[
\mathfrak m=\{x\in R:|x|_p<1\}.
\]
We claim that \(\mathfrak m=pR\). If \(x=py\) with \(y\in R\), then
\[
|x|_p=|p|_p|y|_p\le p^{-1}<1,
\]
so \(pR\subseteq\mathfrak m\). Conversely, let \(x\in\mathfrak m\). If \(x=0\), then plainly \(x\in pR\). If \(x\ne0\), write \(|x|_p=p^{-n}\) for the integer \(n=v_p(x)\). Since \(|x|_p<1\), we have \(n\ge1\), and hence
\[
|x/p|_p=|x|_p/|p|_p=p^{-(n-1)}\le1.
\]
Therefore \(x/p\in R\), and \(x=p(x/p)\in pR\). This proves \(\mathfrak m=pR\). In particular, \(\mathfrak m\) is an ideal of \(R\), and it is proper because \(1\notin\mathfrak m\).

We next determine the units of \(R\). If \(x\in R\) and \(|x|_p=1\), then \(|x^{-1}|_p=|x|_p^{-1}=1\), so \(x^{-1}\in R\); thus \(x\) is a unit of \(R\). Conversely, if \(x\) is a unit of \(R\), then both \(x\) and \(x^{-1}\) belong to \(R\). Consequently \(|x|_p\le1\) and \(|x^{-1}|_p\le1\), while
\[
1=|1|_p=|xx^{-1}|_p=|x|_p|x^{-1}|_p.
\]
These relations force \(|x|_p=1\). Hence the nonunits of \(R\) are exactly the elements of \(\mathfrak m=pR\).

Let \(I\) be any proper ideal of \(R\). It cannot contain a unit, since an ideal containing a unit contains \(1\) and is therefore all of \(R\). Thus every element of \(I\) is a nonunit, so \(I\subseteq\mathfrak m\). On the other hand, if an ideal \(J\) properly contains \(\mathfrak m\), then \(J\) contains some element outside \(\mathfrak m\); that element is a unit, and therefore \(J=R\). Hence \(\mathfrak m\) is maximal. Every maximal ideal is a proper ideal and is consequently contained in \(\mathfrak m\); by maximality it must equal \(\mathfrak m\). Therefore \(p\mathbb Z_p\) is the unique maximal ideal of \(\mathbb Z_p\), proving (b). Since a commutative ring with exactly one maximal ideal is local, \(\mathbb Z_p\) is a local ring, proving (a).
